title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Agents given a plain scraping instruction violate site policies, but adding explicit legal warnings and policy text makes them comply.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, top-to-bottom chat flow, red violation vs green compliance boxes
description: Two parallel panels compare the same scraping task under different prompts. A header row at the top has three link icons: ScrapeBench Website, Evaluation Code and Project Data. The left panel is titled 'Baseline Prompt (No Legal Resources Provided)'. It has a gray user prompt box asking to scrape the New York Times landing page, with a thinking-person avatar beside it. Below is a blue assistant bubble with a robot icon and an HTML file icon. The assistant says it scraped the site and offers to fetch more pages. A red box with a warning triangle labeled 'LEGAL VIOLATION' sits at the bottom. The right panel is titled 'Strong Legal Warning Prompt (ToS and robots.txt Provided)'. Its prompt is longer, with bolded legal warnings and ToS and robots.txt icons. The assistant refuses, and a green 'LEGAL COMPLIANCE' box with a check mark closes the panel. The red and green boxes draw the eye first.
caption: Task Overview. Most AI agents tend to violate the legal policies of popular websites when instructed to scrape their landing page. Inserting into the prompt a strong legal warning and the text of the website's terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt generally results in higher levels of compliance, as schematically illustrated in this figure.
abstract: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and robots$.$txt directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (below 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and robots$.$txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.
